record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own polynomial-regression model-complexity sweep as a test of the general double-descent curve, using a different model and procedure from the original deep-network studies.
record.gate_note: The polynomial-regression sweep reports test-error behavior across model degrees. The neural-network section describes a possible Bayesian extension and computational challenges, but reports no neural-network experiment. The text also discusses other claims and results from cited work; those are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper runs its own minimum-norm polynomial-regression degree sweep (n = 20, degrees 1–50) and reports the test-error curve. This bears on V4, the general curve beyond deep networks, in a new model class. The rest of the paper is theoretical Bayesian argument without risk results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors argue that double descent has a natural Bayesian interpretation. In their account it is driven by the conditional prior p(θ|M) acting as regularization, and it is not in conflict with the Occam's razor of the marginal likelihood. Their only empirical illustration is a frequentist min-norm polynomial sweep showing re-descent. The Bayesian polynomial and neural-network treatments are presented as frameworks or extensions, with no risk experiments.
record.recipe_differences: The reported sweep uses ordinary least squares with a Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse for polynomial regression, rather than testing the original deep-network settings; the Bayesian neural-network discussion is not experimentally evaluated.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 5 shows the log marginal likelihood across assumed polynomial complexity m (up to about 15) for N = 20, peaking at an intermediate complexity. This is Bayesian evidence, not test risk.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bayesian marginal likelihood favours lower-complexity models (Occam's razor) even where the min-norm risk re-descends.

record.problems: The reported sweep is described qualitatively, without numerical test-error values or uncertainty estimates. The stated experiment is a polynomial-regression example, not a neural-network test of the Bayesian framework.

untested.parts: No deep-network model-size sweep. The neural-network section is a proposed extension with no experiment.
Sample size is fixed at n = 20 and never varied.
Only polynomial regression with one data-generating function, one noise level and one seed is tested. Other model classes are asserted from the literature, not tested.
No effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
Noise and regularization are not varied. The claim that the prior/regularization drives double descent is argued theoretically with no risk curves under tuned shrinkage.
No re-measurement against an effective parameter count.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3. Polynomial min-norm regression is a new setting for the general curve rather than a different method aimed at the original deep-network question. The paper says double descent 'may be partly a mirage' of regularization specification, which touches V6/V7, but it is argued, not tested. It is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No deep-network model-size sweep is reported.
No sweep over training epochs or training time is reported.
Training sample size is not varied near the interpolation threshold.
The reported test is limited to polynomial regression with the stated data generation and fitting procedure; other model classes are not tested.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
Noise and regularization are not varied to test peak mechanisms, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not remeasure complexity using an effective parameter count to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: polynomial regression using Legendre polynomial basis functions
rows.operation_detail: Sweep polynomial degree and report training and test MSE using the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse.
rows.value: The text describes test error falling in the low-degree regime, peaking around the interpolation threshold (d ≈ n = 20), then decreasing again for very high degrees (d > 30); degree 50 is reported to perform better than at the interpolation threshold.
rows.note: The paper gives a qualitative description of the sweep and its phases, not numerical test-MSE values. It also describes degree 1 as a poor fit, degree 5 as the classical optimum, degree 20 as the interpolation threshold, and degree 50 as improved over the threshold.
rows.check: The link and state are correct. The result is one illustrative run reported only qualitatively from Figures 2–3: no numbers, no repeats, no uncertainty. The fit is the frequentist pseudoinverse (min-norm) fit, not the Bayesian estimator the paper advocates. The text also misnames d > n as 'overdetermined'.
